statement: Every integer $n > 1$ is a product of [prime numbers](c:prime-number), and this [prime factorization](c:prime-factorization) is unique up to the order of the factors: two products of primes that equal $n$ contain the same primes with the same multiplicities.

hypotheses.text: The integer $n$ satisfies $n > 1$.

conclusion: There are primes $p_1, \dots, p_r$ with $n = p_1 \cdots p_r$, and any primes $q_1, \dots, q_s$ with $n = q_1 \cdots q_s$ are the same list after reordering.

formal.difference: The declaration states only uniqueness, for every natural number $n$: a list of primes with product $n$ is a permutation of the canonical list Nat.primeFactorsList n. Existence is the separate declaration Nat.prod_primeFactorsList.

proofs.name: Least prime factors and cancellation
proofs.slogan: Build a canonical factorization from least prime factors, then match any other factorization with it by Euclid's lemma and cancellation.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; for $n = 1$ both lists are empty, which is the convention for the empty product. Step 3 proves Euclid's lemma from Bézout's identity.

roles.why: Because $n > 1$, the number $n$ has a divisor greater than $1$, so a least one exists and the factorization starts.

steps.slogan: Show that the least divisor $p > 1$ of $n$ is a [prime number](c:prime-number).
steps.detail: The set of divisors of $n$ greater than $1$ contains $n$, so it has a least element $p$. A divisor $d$ of $p$ with $1 < d < p$ would also [divide](c:divisibility) $n$ and be smaller than $p$. So $p$ is prime.

steps.slogan: Split off the least prime factor and factor the cofactor by strong induction.
steps.detail: Write $n = pm$ with $p$ from step 1. If $m = 1$, then $n = p$; if $m > 1$, then $m < n$, so $m$ is a product of primes by induction, and so is $n$. This gives the canonical list of least prime factors.

steps.slogan: Derive Euclid's lemma from Bézout's identity: a prime dividing $ab$ divides $a$ or $b$.
steps.detail: Let the prime $p$ divide $ab$ but not $a$. Then the [greatest common divisor](c:greatest-common-divisor) of $p$ and $a$ is $1$, so Bézout's identity gives integers $x, y$ with $px + ay = 1$. Then $b = pbx + aby$ is divisible by $p$.

steps.slogan: Match each prime of another factorization with a canonical prime and cancel it.
steps.detail: Let $q_1 \cdots q_s = n$ with all $q_j$ prime, and let $p_1 \cdots p_r$ be the list of step 2. By step 3 and induction on $r$, $q_1$ divides some $p_i$, so $q_1 = p_i$. Cancel both and induct on $s$; the empty product $1$ has no prime divisor, so the lists end together.

concepts.c:prime-number: The factors are primes, which cannot be split further.
concepts.c:prime-factorization: The theorem asserts that this factorization exists and is unique.
concepts.c:divisibility: Divisibility drives both the least-divisor step and the cancellation.
concepts.c:greatest-common-divisor: A greatest common divisor $1$ lets Bézout's identity prove Euclid's lemma.

statement: Let $p = (p_1, \dots, p_n)$ and $q = (q_1, \dots, q_n)$ be [probability distributions](c:probability-distribution) with $q_i > 0$ whenever $p_i > 0$. Then the [Kullback–Leibler divergence](c:kullback-leibler-divergence) $D(p \,\|\, q) = \sum_{p_i > 0} p_i \log(p_i/q_i)$ is nonnegative, and it is $0$ only when $p = q$.

hypotheses.text: The vectors $p$ and $q$ are [probability distributions](c:probability-distribution) on $\{1, \dots, n\}$: nonnegative entries with sum $1$.
Every $i$ with $p_i > 0$ has $q_i > 0$.

conclusion: $\sum_{p_i > 0} p_i \log(p_i/q_i) \ge 0$, with equality if and only if $p = q$.

formal.difference:
The declaration works with finite measures $\mu \ll 
u$ and an integrable log-likelihood ratio and proves $\int \log rac{d\mu}{d
u}\,d\mu + 
u(X) - \mu(X) \ge 0$, which is $D \ge 0$ for probability measures. It does not state the equality case.

proofs.name: Pointwise convex function
proofs.slogan: Write the divergence as a weighted sum of values of $\phi(x) = x \log x + 1 - x$, which is nonnegative with its only zero at $1$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, with the equality case. Terms with $p_i = 0$ contribute $0$ by the convention $0 \log 0 = 0$.

roles.why: The sums $\sum p_i = \sum q_i = 1$ cancel the linear terms of $\phi$ and force $p = q$ in the equality case.
Every $i$ with $p_i > 0$ lies in $S = \{i : q_i > 0\}$, so the ratios $p_i/q_i$ are defined.

steps.slogan: Show that the [convex function](c:convex-function) $\phi$ has its strict minimum $0$ at $1$.
steps.detail: Let $\phi(x) = x \log x + 1 - x$ on $[0, \infty)$, with $\phi(0) = 1$. Its derivative is $\log x$ and its second derivative $1/x > 0$, so $\phi$ is strictly convex with $\phi'(1) = 0$. Hence $\phi \ge \phi(1) = 0$, with equality only at $x = 1$.

steps.slogan: Rewrite the divergence as a sum of terms $q_i \phi(p_i/q_i)$ with $q_i > 0$.
steps.detail: Let $S = \{i : q_i > 0\}$; it contains every $i$ with $p_i > 0$. Then $\sum_{i \in S} q_i \phi(p_i/q_i) = \sum_{p_i > 0} p_i \log(p_i/q_i) + \sum_{i \in S} q_i - \sum_{i \in S} p_i$, and both last sums equal $1$.

steps.slogan: Add the nonnegative terms and find when their sum vanishes.
steps.detail: By step 1 each term $q_i \phi(p_i/q_i)$ is at least $0$, so $D(p \,\|\, q) \ge 0$. If $D = 0$, every term vanishes, so $p_i = q_i$ on $S$, and $\sum_{i \notin S} p_i = 0$ gives $p = q$. Conversely $p = q$ makes every logarithm $0$.

concepts.c:probability-distribution: Both distributions sum to one, which cancels the linear terms of $\phi$.
concepts.c:kullback-leibler-divergence: The divergence is the quantity shown to be nonnegative.
concepts.c:convex-function: Strict convexity of $\phi$ gives nonnegativity and the equality case.

proofs.name: Jensen's inequality for the logarithm
proofs.slogan: Apply Jensen's inequality to the concave logarithm with weights $p_i$ to bound $-D(p \,\|\, q)$ by $\log \sum q_i \le 0$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; the equality case uses the strict form of Jensen's inequality.

roles.why: The weights $p_i$ sum to $1$, and $\sum q_i \le 1$ bounds the [logarithm](c:logarithm) by $0$.
The ratios $q_i/p_i$ are positive where $p_i > 0$, so their logarithms are finite.

steps.slogan: Write $-D(p \,\|\, q)$ as the $p$-weighted mean of $\log(q_i/p_i)$ over $P = \{i : p_i > 0\}$.
steps.detail: By definition $-D(p \,\|\, q) = \sum_{i \in P} p_i \log(q_i/p_i)$. Each $q_i/p_i$ with $i \in P$ is positive by the support hypothesis, so each term is finite.

steps.slogan: Move the mean inside the concave [logarithm](c:logarithm) by Jensen's inequality.
steps.detail: The logarithm is strictly concave and the weights $p_i$, $i \in P$, sum to $1$. Jensen's inequality gives $\sum_{i \in P} p_i \log(q_i/p_i) \le \log \sum_{i \in P} q_i$, with equality only when $q_i/p_i$ is constant on $P$.

steps.slogan: Bound the logarithm of the partial sum of $q$ by $\log 1 = 0$.
steps.detail: Since $\sum_{i \in P} q_i \le 1$, the logarithm is at most $0$, so $D(p \,\|\, q) \ge 0$. Equality forces $q_i = c\,p_i$ on $P$ and $\sum_{i \in P} q_i = 1$, so $c = 1$ and $q$ vanishes off $P$; hence $p = q$.

concepts.c:probability-distribution: The entries of $p$ serve as the weights of the mean.
concepts.c:kullback-leibler-divergence: Its negative is the mean that Jensen's inequality bounds.
concepts.c:logarithm: Concavity of the logarithm drives the Jensen step.

source.note: The classical proof by Jensen's inequality, as in Cover and Thomas, Elements of Information Theory, theorem 2.6.3 (information inequality).

statement: Let $K$ be an [algebraically closed field](c:algebraically-closed-field) and $I$ an [ideal](c:ideal) of the [polynomial ring](c:polynomial-ring) $K[x_1, \dots, x_n]$. A polynomial $f$ vanishes at every common zero of $I$ in $K^n$ if and only if $f^m \in I$ for some $m \ge 1$. In other words, $I(V(I))$ equals the [radical](c:radical-ideal) $\sqrt{I}$.

hypotheses.text: The field $K$ is [algebraically closed](c:algebraically-closed-field).
The [polynomial ring](c:polynomial-ring) has finitely many variables $x_1, \dots, x_n$.

conclusion: $I(V(I)) = \sqrt{I}$, where $V(I) \subseteq K^n$ is the set of common zeros of $I$ and $I(V(I))$ is the ideal of polynomials that vanish on it.

formal.difference: The declaration is more general: the coefficients lie in any subfield $k$ of the algebraically closed field $K$, the variables are indexed by a finite type, and the zeros are taken in $K^\sigma$. With $k = K$ it is this statement.

proofs.name: Maximal ideals are points
proofs.slogan: Identify every maximal ideal with the ideal of a point, and write the radical as the intersection of the maximal ideals that contain $I$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. Steps 2 and 4 rest on Zariski's lemma, which follows from the Artin–Tate lemma or from Noether normalization.

roles.why: An algebraic extension of the algebraically closed field $K$ is $K$ itself, so each residue field is $K$.
With finitely many variables each quotient is a finitely generated algebra, as Zariski's lemma needs.

steps.slogan: Show $\sqrt{I} \subseteq I(V(I))$ by evaluating powers at common zeros.
steps.detail: If $f^m \in I$ and $a \in V(I)$, then $f(a)^m = 0$. A field has no nonzero [nilpotent elements](c:nilpotent-element), so $f(a) = 0$.

steps.slogan: Show that each residue field of the polynomial ring is a finite extension of $K$.
steps.detail: Let $L$ be a field that is a finitely generated $K$-algebra, for example $K[x]/\mathfrak{m}$ for a [maximal ideal](c:maximal-ideal) $\mathfrak{m}$. Zariski's lemma, a consequence of the Artin–Tate lemma, says that $L$ is a finite [field extension](c:field-extension) of $K$.

steps.slogan: Identify each maximal ideal $\mathfrak{m}$ with the ideal of a point $a \in K^n$.
steps.detail: By step 2, $K[x]/\mathfrak{m}$ is algebraic over $K$, so it equals $K$ because $K$ is algebraically closed. Let $a_i \in K$ be the image of $x_i$; then $\mathfrak{m}$ contains the maximal ideal $(x_1 - a_1, \dots, x_n - a_n)$ of polynomials vanishing at $a$, so the two are equal.

steps.slogan: Write $\sqrt{I}$ as the intersection of the maximal ideals that contain $I$.
steps.detail: For a prime $P$ and $g \notin P$, a maximal ideal of $(K[x]/P)[1/g]$ has a residue field finite over $K$ by step 2, so its preimage is a maximal ideal containing $P$ but not $g$. So every prime, and hence $\sqrt{I}$, is an intersection of maximal ideals: $K[x]$ is a [Jacobson ring](c:is-jacobson-ring).

steps.slogan: Show that a polynomial vanishing on $V(I)$ lies in every maximal ideal containing $I$.
steps.detail: Let $f \in I(V(I))$ and $\mathfrak{m} \supseteq I$ maximal. By step 3, $\mathfrak{m}$ is the ideal of a point $a$, and $a \in V(I)$ because $I \subseteq \mathfrak{m}$; so $f(a) = 0$ and $f \in \mathfrak{m}$. Step 4 gives $f \in \sqrt{I}$, and step 1 gives the other inclusion.

concepts.c:algebraically-closed-field: Algebraic closedness makes every residue field equal to $K$.
concepts.c:ideal: The theorem describes the polynomials that vanish on the zeros of $I$.
concepts.c:polynomial-ring: The polynomial ring is where both ideals of the identity live.
concepts.c:radical-ideal: The radical is the algebraic answer to the geometric question.
concepts.c:nilpotent-element: Fields have no nilpotents, so a vanishing power forces vanishing.
concepts.c:maximal-ideal: Maximal ideals correspond to the points of $K^n$.
concepts.c:field-extension: Zariski's lemma makes residue fields finite extensions of $K$.
concepts.c:is-jacobson-ring: The Jacobson property turns the radical into an intersection of maximal ideals.

proofs.name: Rabinowitsch trick
proofs.slogan: Derive the strong form from the weak Nullstellensatz by adding a variable $y$ and the relation $1 - yf$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; the case $f = 0$ is trivial. Step 1 rests on Zariski's lemma.

roles.why: It gives every proper ideal a common zero in step 1.
With finitely many variables, $K[x, y]$ is again a polynomial ring in finitely many variables, so step 1 applies to it.

steps.slogan: Prove the weak Nullstellensatz: every proper ideal has a common zero.
steps.detail: A proper ideal $J$ lies in a [maximal ideal](c:maximal-ideal) $\mathfrak{m}$. By Zariski's lemma, $K[x]/\mathfrak{m}$ is a finite extension of $K$, so it equals $K$. The images $a_i$ of the variables give a point $a$ at which every element of $J$ vanishes.

steps.slogan: Show $\sqrt{I} \subseteq I(V(I))$ by evaluating powers at common zeros.
steps.detail: If $f^m \in I$ and $a \in V(I)$, then $f(a)^m = 0$. A field has no nonzero [nilpotent elements](c:nilpotent-element), so $f(a) = 0$.

steps.slogan: Add a variable $y$ and show that $I + (1 - yf)$ has no common zero.
steps.detail: Let $f \in I(V(I))$ and $J = I + (1 - yf)$ in $K[x_1, \dots, x_n, y]$. At a common zero $(a, b)$ of $J$ we have $a \in V(I)$, so $f(a) = 0$ and $1 - b f(a) = 1 \ne 0$. So $J$ has no zero, and step 1 gives $1 \in J$.

steps.slogan: Substitute $y = 1/f$ and clear denominators to get $f^m \in I$.
steps.detail: Write $1 = \sum_i g_i(x, y) h_i(x) + g_0(x, y)(1 - yf)$ with $h_i \in I$. Put $y = 1/f$ in the field of rational functions and multiply by $f^m$, where $m$ bounds the $y$-degrees of the $g_i$. This gives $f^m = \sum_i \tilde g_i(x) h_i(x) \in I$.

steps.slogan: Combine the two inclusions into $I(V(I)) = \sqrt{I}$.
steps.detail: Steps 3 and 4 show that every $f \in I(V(I))$ has a power in $I$, so $I(V(I)) \subseteq \sqrt{I}$. Step 2 gives the reverse inclusion.

concepts.c:algebraically-closed-field: Algebraic closedness makes every residue field equal to $K$.
concepts.c:ideal: The theorem describes the polynomials that vanish on the zeros of $I$.
concepts.c:polynomial-ring: The polynomial ring is where both ideals of the identity live.
concepts.c:radical-ideal: The radical is the algebraic answer to the geometric question.
concepts.c:nilpotent-element: Fields have no nilpotents, so a vanishing power forces vanishing.
concepts.c:maximal-ideal: A maximal ideal above a proper ideal supplies the common zero.

source.note: Rabinowitsch's trick (1930), as in Cox, Little and O'Shea, Ideals, Varieties, and Algorithms, chapter 4, section 1.

statement: Let $(X, \mu)$ be a [measure space](c:measure-space) and let $p, q > 1$ be [Hölder conjugate exponents](c:holder-conjugate-exponents), $1/p + 1/q = 1$. For measurable $f, g\colon X \to [0, \infty)$, $\int fg\,d\mu \le \left(\int f^p\,d\mu\right)^{1/p} \left(\int g^q\,d\mu\right)^{1/q}$, where the [Lebesgue integrals](c:lebesgue-integral) take values in $[0, \infty]$.

hypotheses.text: The exponents satisfy $p, q > 1$ and $1/p + 1/q = 1$.
The functions $f, g\colon X \to [0, \infty)$ are measurable.

conclusion: $\int fg\,d\mu \le \|f\|_p \|g\|_q$, the product of the [Lp](c:lp-space) norms of $f$ and $g$.

formal.difference: The declaration asks only that $f$ and $g$ are almost everywhere measurable; otherwise it states the same inequality for lower Lebesgue integrals.

proofs.name: Normalize and integrate Young's inequality
proofs.slogan: Normalize both functions to unit norm, apply Young's inequality at each point, and integrate.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. Zero and infinite norms are handled first; the main case has $0 < \|f\|_p, \|g\|_q < \infty$.

roles.why: The relation $1/p + 1/q = 1$ makes Young's inequality hold and the integrated bound equal to $1$.
Measurability makes the integrals defined, and a zero integral of $f^p$ forces $f = 0$ almost everywhere.

steps.slogan: Dispose of the cases where a norm is zero or infinite.
steps.detail: Let $A = (\int f^p)^{1/p}$ and $B = (\int g^q)^{1/q}$. If $A = 0$, then $f = 0$ almost everywhere, so the left side is $0$; the case $B = 0$ is the same. If both are nonzero and one is infinite, the right side is $\infty$.

steps.slogan: Prove Young's inequality $ab \le a^p/p + b^q/q$ for $a, b \ge 0$.
steps.detail: The case $ab = 0$ is trivial. For $a, b > 0$, concavity of the logarithm with weights $1/p$ and $1/q$ gives $\log(a^p/p + b^q/q) \ge \frac{1}{p}\log a^p + \frac{1}{q}\log b^q = \log(ab)$.

steps.slogan: Divide $f$ by $A$ and $g$ by $B$ to get unit norms.
steps.detail: In the remaining case $0 < A, B < \infty$, the functions $F = f/A$ and $G = g/B$ satisfy $\int F^p\,d\mu = \int G^q\,d\mu = 1$. Both sides of the inequality scale in the same way, so it suffices to show $\int FG\,d\mu \le 1$.

steps.slogan: Integrate Young's inequality for $F(x)$ and $G(x)$ over $X$.
steps.detail: At each point $FG \le F^p/p + G^q/q$, so the [Lebesgue integral](c:lebesgue-integral) gives $\int FG\,d\mu \le 1/p + 1/q = 1$. Multiplying by $AB$ gives $\int fg\,d\mu \le AB$.

concepts.c:measure-space: The inequality holds on any measure space, finite or not.
concepts.c:holder-conjugate-exponents: Conjugacy makes the integrated Young bound exactly one.
concepts.c:lebesgue-integral: Monotonicity and linearity of the integral carry the pointwise bound.
concepts.c:lp-space: The right side is the product of the two Lp norms.

statement: For every real $m \times n$ matrix $A$, the payoff matrix of a two-player [zero-sum game](c:zero-sum-game), $\max_{x \in \Delta_m} \min_{y \in \Delta_n} x^{\top} A y = \min_{y \in \Delta_n} \max_{x \in \Delta_m} x^{\top} A y$. Here $\Delta_k$ is the [simplex](c:simplex) of probability vectors in $\mathbb{R}^k$, the set of [mixed strategies](c:mixed-strategy).

hypotheses.text: The game has finitely many pure strategies, $m, n \ge 1$, and a real payoff matrix $A$.
Both players use [mixed strategies](c:mixed-strategy), points of the [convex](c:convex-set) and [compact](c:compact-space) simplices $\Delta_m$ and $\Delta_n$.

conclusion: The max-min value $v_1$ equals the min-max value $v_2$, and both extrema are attained.

proofs.name: Theorem of the alternative
proofs.slogan: Separate the origin from the convex hull of the columns and the unit vectors to show that $v_1 < v_2$ is impossible.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The inequality $v_1 \le v_2$ holds for every payoff function; the separation argument gives the reverse.

roles.why: Finitely many strategies make the payoffs finitely many linear functions on $\mathbb{R}^m$, where separation works.
The simplices are compact for the extrema and convex, so normalized combinations are mixed strategies.

steps.slogan: Show that the maxima and minima exist on the compact simplices.
steps.detail: The map $x \mapsto \min_y x^{\top} A y = \min_j (x^{\top} A)_j$ is a minimum of finitely many linear functions, so it is continuous. The simplex $\Delta_m$ is nonempty and [compact](c:compact-space), so the maximum $v_1$ exists; in the same way $v_2$ exists.

steps.slogan: Prove the max-min inequality $v_1 \le v_2$ by comparing at a common pair.
steps.detail: For all $x \in \Delta_m$ and $y \in \Delta_n$, $\min_{y'} x^{\top} A y' \le x^{\top} A y \le \max_{x'} x'^{\top} A y$. Take the maximum over $x$ on the left and the minimum over $y$ on the right.

steps.slogan: Separate the origin from the [convex hull](c:convex-hull) of the columns and the unit vectors.
steps.detail: Let $C$ be the convex hull of the columns of $A$ and the unit vectors $e_i$. If $0 \in C$, normalizing the column weights gives $y \in \Delta_n$ with $Ay \le 0$, so $v_2 \le 0$. Otherwise a [separating hyperplane](c:separating-hyperplane) gives $x$ with $x \cdot c > 0$ on $C$, so $x > 0$ and its normalization has $x^{\top} A > 0$, so $v_1 > 0$.

steps.slogan: Apply the alternative to the shifted matrix $A - cJ$ for each real $c$.
steps.detail: Let $J$ be the all-ones matrix. For probability vectors $x^{\top} J y = 1$, so both values of $A - cJ$ are those of $A$ minus $c$. Step 3 gives, for every real $c$, either $v_2 \le c$ or $v_1 > c$.

steps.slogan: Choose $c$ strictly between $v_1$ and $v_2$ to exclude $v_1 < v_2$.
steps.detail: If $v_1 < v_2$, the number $c = (v_1 + v_2)/2$ has $v_2 > c$ and $v_1 < c$, which contradicts step 4. So $v_1 \ge v_2$, and step 2 gives $v_1 = v_2$.

concepts.c:zero-sum-game: The matrix lists one player's gain, which is the other's loss.
concepts.c:simplex: Mixed strategies form simplices, which are compact and convex.
concepts.c:mixed-strategy: Mixing pure strategies makes the payoff bilinear on convex sets.
concepts.c:convex-set: Convexity keeps normalized combinations inside the strategy sets.
concepts.c:compact-space: Compactness of the simplices makes the extrema attained.
concepts.c:convex-hull: The hull of columns and unit vectors carries the alternative.
concepts.c:separating-hyperplane: Separation from the origin yields a strategy with positive payoffs.

source.note: The classical proof through the theorem of the alternative for matrices, as in von Neumann and Morgenstern, Theory of Games and Economic Behavior (1944), chapter III.

statement: Let $A$ be a real $n \times n$ matrix, $n \ge 1$, with all entries positive. Then its [spectral radius](c:spectral-radius) $r$ is a positive [eigenvalue](c:eigenvalue) with an [eigenvector](c:eigenvector) whose entries are all positive, $r$ is a simple root of the [characteristic polynomial](c:characteristic-polynomial), and every other complex eigenvalue $\lambda$ satisfies $|\lambda| < r$.

hypotheses.text: The matrix $A$ is a real $n \times n$ matrix with $n \ge 1$.
Every entry $a_{ij}$ of $A$ is positive, so $A$ is a strictly positive [nonnegative matrix](c:nonnegative-matrix).

conclusion: The number $r = \rho(A) > 0$ is a simple eigenvalue with a positive eigenvector, and $|\lambda| < r$ for every eigenvalue $\lambda \ne r$.

proofs.name: Collatz–Wielandt maximization
proofs.slogan: Maximize the largest $t$ with $Ax \ge tx$ over nonnegative vectors, show that a maximizer is a positive eigenvector, and compare every other eigenvalue with it.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; for $n = 1$ every step is immediate. Inequalities between vectors hold entry by entry.

roles.why: A square matrix has eigenvalues and a characteristic polynomial, and $n \ge 1$ makes the simplex of nonnegative unit-sum vectors nonempty.
Positivity sends every nonzero nonnegative vector to a positive vector and forces the equality cases to align.

steps.slogan: Maximize the Collatz–Wielandt ratio $t(x) = \min_i (Ax)_i/x_i$ over nonnegative vectors.
steps.detail: For $x \ge 0$, $x \ne 0$, let $t(x)$ be the largest $t$ with $Ax \ge tx$. Since $t(Ax) \ge t(x)$ and $t$ is continuous on the compact set $A(\Delta)$ of positive vectors, $t$ attains its supremum $r$ at some $x$, and $r \ge \min_i \sum_j a_{ij} > 0$.

steps.slogan: Show that a maximizer $x$ is a positive [eigenvector](c:eigenvector) for $r$.
steps.detail: Let $w = Ax - rx \ge 0$. If $w \ne 0$, then $Aw > 0$, so $y = Ax$ satisfies $Ay > ry$ and $t(y) > r$, against maximality. So $Ax = rx$ and $x = Ax/r > 0$; in the same way every nonnegative $z \ne 0$ with $Az \ge rz$ is a positive eigenvector.

steps.slogan: Show that $r$ is a simple root of the [characteristic polynomial](c:characteristic-polynomial).
steps.detail: If a real eigenvector $w$ for $r$ is not a multiple of $x$, some $x - cw \ge 0$ is a nonzero eigenvector with a zero entry, against step 2; so the eigenspace is a line. Steps 1 and 2 for $A^{\top}$ give $u > 0$ with $u^{\top} A = r u^{\top}$, and a Jordan chain $(A - rI)w = x$ would give $0 = u^{\top} x > 0$.

steps.slogan: Bound every eigenvalue by $r$ with the triangle inequality.
steps.detail: If $Az = \lambda z$ with $z \in \mathbb{C}^n$ nonzero, then $|\lambda|\,|z| = |Az| \le A|z|$ entry by entry. So $t(|z|) \ge |\lambda|$, hence $|\lambda| \le r$, and $r$ is the [spectral radius](c:spectral-radius).

steps.slogan: Show that an eigenvalue with $|\lambda| = r$ equals $r$.
steps.detail: If $|\lambda| = r$, step 4 gives $A|z| \ge r|z|$, so step 2 gives $A|z| = r|z|$, and step 3 makes $|z|$ a positive multiple of $x$. Then $|\sum_j a_{ij} z_j| = \sum_j a_{ij} |z_j|$ with all $a_{ij} > 0$, so $z = e^{i\theta}|z|$ for one angle $\theta$, and $\lambda = r$.

concepts.c:spectral-radius: The largest eigenvalue modulus turns out to be the maximized ratio.
concepts.c:eigenvalue: The theorem locates the dominant eigenvalue and isolates it.
concepts.c:eigenvector: The maximizer is the positive Perron eigenvector.
concepts.c:characteristic-polynomial: Simplicity concerns the multiplicity of $r$ as a root.
concepts.c:nonnegative-matrix: Strict positivity of the entries forces strict inequalities in each step.

source.note: Wielandt's proof by the Collatz–Wielandt function, as in Horn and Johnson, Matrix Analysis, chapter 8.

statement: In a [right triangle](c:right-triangle) with legs of lengths $a$ and $b$ and hypotenuse of length $c$, $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$.

hypotheses.text: The triangle $ABC$ lies in a [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space), with side lengths given by the [Euclidean distance](c:euclidean-distance).
The [angle](c:angle) at $C$ is a right angle, and $a = BC$, $b = CA$, $c = AB$.

formal.difference: The declaration states an equivalence, so it also gives the converse: the relation between the squared distances forces a right angle. It holds in every real inner product space, with the right angle at the middle point $p_2$.

proofs.name: Expand the inner product
proofs.slogan: Write the legs as vectors from the right-angle vertex and expand the squared length of their difference; the cross term vanishes.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for a nondegenerate triangle in any Euclidean space.

roles.why: The Euclidean distance is the norm of an [inner product](c:inner-product-space), which can be expanded.
A right angle at $C$ means that the two leg vectors are orthogonal.

steps.slogan: Write the legs as the vectors $u = A - C$ and $v = B - C$.
steps.detail: In a Euclidean space the [Euclidean distance](c:euclidean-distance) is the norm of a difference, so $b = \|u\|$, $a = \|v\|$ and $c = \|A - B\| = \|u - v\|$.

steps.slogan: Expand $\|u - v\|^2$ by bilinearity of the [inner product](c:inner-product-space).
steps.detail: The norm comes from the inner product, so $\|u - v\|^2 = \langle u - v, u - v \rangle = \|u\|^2 - 2\langle u, v \rangle + \|v\|^2$ by bilinearity and symmetry.

steps.slogan: Translate the right angle at $C$ into $\langle u, v \rangle = 0$.
steps.detail: The angle at $C$ is $\arccos(\langle u, v \rangle / (\|u\|\,\|v\|))$, with $u, v \ne 0$ for a triangle. It equals $\pi/2$ exactly when $\langle u, v \rangle = 0$, that is, when the legs are [orthogonal](c:orthogonality).

steps.slogan: Drop the zero cross term to get $c^2 = a^2 + b^2$.
steps.detail: Substituting $\langle u, v \rangle = 0$ into step 2 gives $\|u - v\|^2 = \|u\|^2 + \|v\|^2$. By step 1 this reads $c^2 = b^2 + a^2$.

concepts.c:right-triangle: The theorem concerns exactly the triangles with one right angle.
concepts.c:euclidean-space: The space supplies the inner product behind lengths and angles.
concepts.c:euclidean-distance: Side lengths are norms of difference vectors.
concepts.c:angle: The angle at $C$ is defined through the inner product.
concepts.c:inner-product-space: Bilinear expansion of the inner product produces the cross term.
concepts.c:orthogonality: Orthogonal legs make the cross term vanish.

source.note: mathlib rewrites distances as norms of differences (dist_eq_norm_vsub) and applies norm_sub_sq_eq_norm_sq_add_norm_sq_iff_angle_eq_pi_div_two, which expands the norm and uses inner_eq_zero_iff_angle_eq_pi_div_two.

proofs.name: Altitude and similar triangles
proofs.slogan: Drop the altitude to the hypotenuse, which cuts the triangle into two triangles similar to it, and add the two ratio equations.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The right angle makes the other two angles acute, so the foot of the altitude lies between $A$ and $B$.

roles.why: Euclidean geometry gives the angle sum $\pi$ and the angle-angle criterion for [similar triangles](c:similar-triangles).
The right angle at $C$ matches the right angles at the foot $H$ and makes the other angles acute.

steps.slogan: Drop the altitude from $C$ to the hypotenuse with foot $H$.
steps.detail: The angles at $A$ and $B$ add up to $\pi/2$, so both are acute. Hence $H$ lies between $A$ and $B$, and $AH + HB = c$.

steps.slogan: Show that the triangles $ACH$ and $CBH$ are similar to $ABC$.
steps.detail: Triangles $ACH$ and $ABC$ share the angle at $A$, and each has a right angle, at $H$ and at $C$. By the angle-angle criterion they are [similar](c:similar-triangles); in the same way $CBH$ and $ABC$ share the angle at $B$.

steps.slogan: Equate ratios of matching sides to get $b^2 = c \cdot AH$ and $a^2 = c \cdot HB$.
steps.detail: From $ACH \sim ABC$, $AC/AB = AH/AC$, so $b^2 = c \cdot AH$. From $CBH \sim ABC$, $BC/AB = HB/BC$, so $a^2 = c \cdot HB$.

steps.slogan: Add the two equations and use $AH + HB = c$.
steps.detail: Adding gives $a^2 + b^2 = c\,(AH + HB)$, and step 1 gives $AH + HB = c$. So $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$.

concepts.c:right-triangle: The right angle is what makes the two parts similar to the whole.
concepts.c:euclidean-space: Euclidean geometry gives the angle sum and the similarity criteria.
concepts.c:euclidean-distance: Side lengths are the distances whose ratios the proof compares.
concepts.c:angle: Equal angles identify the similar triangles.
concepts.c:similar-triangles: Similarity turns equal angles into equal side ratios.

source.note: The classical proof by the altitude and similar triangles; Euclid, Elements, book VI, proposition 8, gives the similarity of the two parts to the whole.

statement: Let $M$ be a smooth [oriented](c:orientation-of-a-manifold) $n$-dimensional [manifold with boundary](c:manifold-with-boundary), $n \ge 1$, with $\partial M$ given the induced orientation, and let $\omega$ be a smooth $(n-1)$-[form](c:differential-form) with compact support. Then the integral of the [exterior derivative](c:exterior-derivative) $d\omega$ over $M$ equals the integral of $\omega$ over $\partial M$: $\int_M d\omega = \int_{\partial M} \omega$.

hypotheses.text: $M$ is a smooth $n$-dimensional [manifold with boundary](c:manifold-with-boundary) with $n \ge 1$.
$M$ is [oriented](c:orientation-of-a-manifold), and $\partial M$ carries the induced outward-normal-first orientation.
$\omega$ is a smooth $(n-1)$-[form](c:differential-form) on $M$ with compact support.

conclusion: $\int_M d\omega = \int_{\partial M} \omega$; in particular $\int_M d\omega = 0$ when $\partial M = \emptyset$.

proofs.name: Half-space computation and partition of unity
proofs.slogan: Prove the formula on the half-space by Fubini and the fundamental theorem of calculus, then glue the charts with a partition of unity.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, with $\partial M = \emptyset$ and $n = 1$, where $\partial M$ is a finite set of signed points. Interior charts map to $\mathbb{R}^n$, where step 1 gives $0$ on both sides.

roles.why: Charts identify $M$ locally with $\mathbb{R}^n$ or the half-space $\mathbb{H}^n$ and carry boundary to boundary.
Oriented charts make the integrals defined and match the boundary orientation of $\mathbb{H}^n$.
Compact support removes the boundary terms at infinity and makes the partition of unity finite.

steps.slogan: Prove the formula for a compactly supported form on the half-space $\mathbb{H}^n$.
steps.detail: Write $\omega = \sum_i \omega_i\, dx_1 \wedge \cdots \widehat{dx_i} \cdots \wedge dx_n$, so $d\omega = \sum_i (-1)^{i-1} \partial_i \omega_i\, dx_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge dx_n$. By Fubini and the fundamental theorem of calculus the terms with $i < n$ integrate to $0$, and the term $i = n$ gives $(-1)^n \int_{\mathbb{R}^{n-1}} \omega_n(x', 0)\,dx' = \int_{\partial \mathbb{H}^n} \omega$.

steps.slogan: Cover the support by finitely many oriented charts and choose a subordinate [partition of unity](c:partition-of-unity).
steps.detail: The support of $\omega$ is compact, so finitely many positively oriented charts onto open sets of $\mathbb{R}^n$ or $\mathbb{H}^n$ cover it. A smooth partition of unity $\psi_1, \dots, \psi_k$ subordinate to them has $\sum_\alpha \psi_\alpha = 1$ on the support.

steps.slogan: Transfer each piece $\psi_\alpha \omega$ to the half-space through its chart.
steps.detail: Integrals of $n$-forms are invariant under orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms, and $d$ commutes with pullback. Charts send boundary to boundary with the induced orientation, so step 1 gives $\int_M d(\psi_\alpha \omega) = \int_{\partial M} \psi_\alpha \omega$.

steps.slogan: Sum the local identities over the finite partition of unity.
steps.detail: Since $\sum_\alpha \psi_\alpha \omega = \omega$, linearity of $d$ gives $\sum_\alpha d(\psi_\alpha \omega) = d\omega$. Summing step 3 over $\alpha$ gives $\int_M d\omega = \sum_\alpha \int_{\partial M} \psi_\alpha \omega = \int_{\partial M} \omega$.

concepts.c:orientation-of-a-manifold: Orientation fixes the signs of both integrals and of the boundary.
concepts.c:manifold-with-boundary: Boundary charts model the manifold on the half-space, where the boundary term appears.
concepts.c:differential-form: Forms are the objects that integrate over oriented manifolds.
concepts.c:exterior-derivative: The derivative $d\omega$ is the form integrated over $M$.
concepts.c:partition-of-unity: It splits $\omega$ into pieces supported in single charts.

source.note: The standard proof, as in J. M. Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds, 2nd edition, theorem 16.11.

statement: The [Gaussian curvature](c:gaussian-curvature) $K$ of a [regular surface](c:regular-surface) $S \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ depends only on its [first fundamental form](c:first-fundamental-form): in local coordinates $K$ is a function of $E, F, G$ and their derivatives up to order two. Hence a local [isometry](c:isometry) $\varphi\colon S \to S'$ satisfies $K'(\varphi(p)) = K(p)$ for every $p \in S$.

hypotheses.text: $S$ and $S'$ are [regular surfaces](c:regular-surface) in $\mathbb{R}^3$, smooth with a unit normal field on each coordinate patch.
The map $\varphi\colon S \to S'$ is a local [isometry](c:isometry): its differential preserves the first fundamental form.

conclusion: $K$ is expressed by $E, F, G$ and their first and second derivatives, so $K'(\varphi(p)) = K(p)$.

proofs.name: Gauss formula from the frame equations
proofs.slogan: Write the second derivatives of a parametrization in the frame $x_u, x_v, N$, and compare mixed third derivatives to express $EK$ through the Christoffel symbols.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, one coordinate patch at a time; the patches cover the surface.

roles.why: Regularity gives a parametrization with independent $x_u, x_v$ and a smooth unit normal, so the frame exists.
An isometry carries a parametrization to one with the same $E, F, G$.

steps.slogan: Expand $x_{uu}$, $x_{uv}$ and $x_{vv}$ in the frame $x_u, x_v, N$.
steps.detail: For a parametrization $x(u, v)$ with unit normal $N$, write $x_{uu} = \Gamma^1_{11} x_u + \Gamma^2_{11} x_v + eN$, $x_{uv} = \Gamma^1_{12} x_u + \Gamma^2_{12} x_v + fN$ and $x_{vv} = \Gamma^1_{22} x_u + \Gamma^2_{22} x_v + gN$. Here $e, f, g$ are the coefficients of the [second fundamental form](c:second-fundamental-form), and $K = (eg - f^2)/(EG - F^2)$.

steps.slogan: Show that the [Christoffel symbols](c:christoffel-symbols) depend only on $E, F, G$ and their first derivatives.
steps.detail: Take inner products of the frame equations with $x_u$ and $x_v$; for example $\Gamma^1_{11} E + \Gamma^2_{11} F = \frac12 E_u$ and $\Gamma^1_{11} F + \Gamma^2_{11} G = F_u - \frac12 E_v$. These linear systems have determinant $EG - F^2 > 0$, so they determine the symbols.

steps.slogan: Compare the $x_v$ components of $(x_{uu})_v$ and $(x_{uv})_u$.
steps.detail: These third derivatives are equal. Expand both with the frame equations and the Weingarten equations for $N_u, N_v$; the $x_v$ component gives the Gauss formula, which writes $-EK$ as a polynomial in the Christoffel symbols and their first derivatives.

steps.slogan: Divide the Gauss formula by $E > 0$ to express $K$ intrinsically.
steps.detail: Since $E = \|x_u\|^2 > 0$, steps 2 and 3 express $K$ through $E, F, G$ and their derivatives up to order two. No term depends on $N$ or on the embedding.

steps.slogan: Transport the parametrization by the local isometry and compare the curvatures.
steps.detail: If $\varphi$ is a local isometry, $y = \varphi \circ x$ parametrizes $S'$ near $\varphi(p)$ with the same $E, F, G$ as $x$. The formula of step 4 then gives $K'(\varphi(p)) = K(p)$.

concepts.c:gaussian-curvature: The curvature is the quantity shown to be intrinsic.
concepts.c:regular-surface: Regular parametrizations give the moving frame of the computation.
concepts.c:first-fundamental-form: Its coefficients $E, F, G$ are the only data in the final formula.
concepts.c:isometry: Isometries preserve $E, F, G$, hence the curvature.
concepts.c:second-fundamental-form: Its coefficients define $K$ but drop out of the final formula.
concepts.c:christoffel-symbols: They carry the intrinsic data into the Gauss formula.

source.note: The classical derivation of the Gauss formula, as in M. do Carmo, Differential Geometry of Curves and Surfaces, section 4-3.

statement: For a [probability measure](c:probability-measure) $P$ and a finite or countable family of events $A_1, A_2, \dots$, the probability of their [countable union](c:countable-union-of-events) is at most the sum of their probabilities: $P\big(\bigcup_i A_i\big) \le \sum_i P(A_i)$.

hypotheses.text: $P$ is a [probability measure](c:probability-measure) on the events, so it is countably additive.
The family of events $A_1, A_2, \dots$ is finite or countable.

conclusion: $P\big(\bigcup_i A_i\big) \le \sum_i P(A_i)$, where the sum may exceed $1$.

formal.difference: The declaration holds for every outer measure, hence for every measure, with values in $[0, \infty]$ and any countable index type. It needs no measurability of the sets.

proofs.name: Disjoint pieces
proofs.slogan: Replace the events by disjoint pieces with the same union, add their probabilities, and bound each piece by its event.
proofs.scope: Finite and countable families; a finite family is extended by empty events. The empty family gives $0 \le 0$.

roles.why: Countable additivity evaluates the disjoint union, and monotonicity compares each piece with its event.
A countable family can be indexed by the natural numbers, so a least index exists and additivity applies.

steps.slogan: Replace the events by the disjoint sets $B_i = A_i \setminus \bigcup_{j < i} A_j$.
steps.detail: Index the events by $i = 1, 2, \dots$. A point of $\bigcup_i A_i$ lies in $B_i$ for the least $i$ with the point in $A_i$, so the $B_i$ are pairwise disjoint, $B_i \subseteq A_i$, and $\bigcup_i B_i = \bigcup_i A_i$.

steps.slogan: Evaluate the union by countable additivity on the disjoint pieces.
steps.detail: The sets $B_i$ are events and pairwise disjoint, so countable additivity of the [measure](c:measure) gives $P\big(\bigcup_i A_i\big) = P\big(\bigcup_i B_i\big) = \sum_i P(B_i)$.

steps.slogan: Bound each term $P(B_i)$ by $P(A_i)$ through monotonicity.
steps.detail: Since $B_i \subseteq A_i$, monotonicity gives $P(B_i) \le P(A_i)$ for every $i$. Summing these nonnegative terms gives $\sum_i P(B_i) \le \sum_i P(A_i)$, which with step 2 is the bound.

concepts.c:probability-measure: Countable additivity of the probability gives the sum over pieces.
concepts.c:countable-union-of-events: The bound controls exactly this union of events.
concepts.c:measure: Additivity and monotonicity of measures carry every step.

statement: Let $V$ be a real [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) and $B$ a bounded [bilinear form](c:bilinear-form) on $V$ that is [coercive](c:coercivity): $B(v, v) \ge c\|v\|^2$ for some $c > 0$. Then for every bounded [linear functional](c:linear-functional) $f$ on $V$ there is a unique $u \in V$, the [weak solution](c:weak-solution), with $B(u, v) = f(v)$ for all $v \in V$, and $\|u\| \le \|f\|/c$.

hypotheses.text: $V$ is a real [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space).
$B$ is bilinear and bounded: $|B(u, v)| \le C\|u\|\,\|v\|$ for some constant $C$.
$B$ is [coercive](c:coercivity): $B(v, v) \ge c\|v\|^2$ for all $v$, with $c > 0$.
$f$ is a bounded [linear functional](c:linear-functional) on $V$.

conclusion: There is exactly one $u \in V$ with $B(u, v) = f(v)$ for all $v \in V$, and $\|u\| \le \|f\|/c$.

formal.difference: The declaration builds the continuous linear equivalence $B^\sharp\colon V \to V$ with $B(v, w) = \langle B^\sharp v, w \rangle$. The weak solution is $u = (B^\sharp)^{-1} w_f$, where $w_f$ represents $f$ by the Riesz theorem, and the bound comes from the separate lemma IsCoercive.antilipschitz.

proofs.name: Riesz operator bounded below
proofs.slogan: Represent the form by an operator through the Riesz theorem, show that coercivity makes it injective with closed and dense range, and invert it.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. Uniqueness and the bound come from the lower bound of step 2.

roles.why: Completeness gives limits of Cauchy sequences, and the inner product gives Riesz representatives and orthogonal complements.
Boundedness makes each $B(v, \cdot)$ a bounded functional and the operator $A$ continuous.
Coercivity bounds $A$ from below and makes the orthogonal complement of its range zero.
The bounded functional $f$ has a Riesz representative $w_f$, which is the right side to invert.

steps.slogan: Represent $B$ by a bounded operator $A$ with $B(v, w) = \langle Av, w \rangle$.
steps.detail: For fixed $v$, the map $w \mapsto B(v, w)$ is a bounded linear functional, so the Riesz representation theorem gives a unique $Av \in V$ with $B(v, w) = \langle Av, w \rangle$. The map $A$ is linear, and $\|Av\| \le C\|v\|$.

steps.slogan: Bound $A$ from below by coercivity and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality.
steps.detail: For every $v$, $c\|v\|^2 \le B(v, v) = \langle Av, v \rangle \le \|Av\|\,\|v\|$, so $\|Av\| \ge c\|v\|$. In particular $A$ is injective.

steps.slogan: Show that the range of $A$ is closed by a Cauchy sequence argument.
steps.detail: If $Av_n \to w$, then $\|v_n - v_m\| \le \|Av_n - Av_m\|/c$, so $(v_n)$ is a [Cauchy sequence](c:cauchy-sequence) and converges to some $v$ by completeness. Continuity of $A$ gives $Av = w$.

steps.slogan: Show that the range has zero [orthogonal](c:orthogonality) complement, so it is all of $V$.
steps.detail: If $\langle Av, w \rangle = 0$ for all $v$, then $v = w$ gives $c\|w\|^2 \le B(w, w) = \langle Aw, w \rangle = 0$, so $w = 0$. By the projection theorem, a closed subspace with zero orthogonal complement is all of $V$.

steps.slogan: Solve $Au = w_f$ for the Riesz representative $w_f$ of $f$.
steps.detail: The Riesz theorem gives $w_f$ with $f(v) = \langle w_f, v \rangle$ and $\|w_f\| = \|f\|$. Since $A$ is bijective, $u = A^{-1} w_f$ satisfies $B(u, v) = \langle Au, v \rangle = f(v)$ for all $v$; it is unique by injectivity, and $\|u\| \le \|Au\|/c = \|f\|/c$.

concepts.c:hilbert-space: Completeness and the inner product drive the Riesz and projection steps.
concepts.c:bilinear-form: The bounded form becomes an operator on the space.
concepts.c:coercivity: Coercivity gives the lower bound and the zero orthogonal complement.
concepts.c:linear-functional: The right side $f$ is represented by a vector.
concepts.c:weak-solution: The solution $u$ satisfies the equation against every test vector.
concepts.c:cauchy-sequence: Preimages of a convergent sequence form a Cauchy sequence.
concepts.c:orthogonality: A zero orthogonal complement makes the closed range everything.

statement: Every [continuous](c:continuous-function) $2\pi$-periodic function $f\colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}$ is a [uniform limit](c:uniform-convergence) of [trigonometric polynomials](c:trigonometric-polynomial) $\sum_{|n| \le N} c_n e^{inx}$: for every $\varepsilon > 0$ some trigonometric polynomial $p$ satisfies $|f(x) - p(x)| < \varepsilon$ for all real $x$.

hypotheses.text: The function $f\colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function).
The function $f$ is $2\pi$-periodic: $f(x + 2\pi) = f(x)$ for all real $x$.

conclusion: For every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a trigonometric polynomial $p$ with $\sup_x |f(x) - p(x)| < \varepsilon$.

formal.difference: The declaration works on the circle $\mathbb{R}/T\mathbb{Z}$ for any period $T > 0$ and states that the span of the monomials $e^{2\pi i n x/T}$ is dense in $C(\mathbb{R}/T\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{C})$ for the sup norm. With $T = 2\pi$ this is the same statement.

proofs.name: Stone–Weierstrass on the circle
proofs.slogan: View $f$ as a continuous function on the compact circle and check that trigonometric polynomials form a point-separating, conjugation-closed unital subalgebra.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; real-valued $f$ is a special case.

roles.why: Continuity makes $f$ an element of $C(\mathbb{T}, \mathbb{C})$, where Stone–Weierstrass applies.
Periodicity lets $f$ factor through the circle $\mathbb{T} = \mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}$.

steps.slogan: Identify $f$ with a continuous function on the compact [circle](c:circle) $\mathbb{T} = \mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}$.
steps.detail: Because $f$ is $2\pi$-periodic, it factors through the quotient $\mathbb{T}$, and the factor is continuous. The circle is a compact Hausdorff space, and uniform approximation on $\mathbb{R}$ is approximation in the sup norm of $C(\mathbb{T}, \mathbb{C})$.

steps.slogan: Check that trigonometric polynomials form a [subalgebra](c:subalgebra) closed under conjugation.
steps.detail: With $e_n(x) = e^{inx}$ we have $e_m e_n = e_{m+n}$, $e_0 = 1$ and $\overline{e_n} = e_{-n}$. So the span of the $e_n$ is a unital subalgebra of $C(\mathbb{T}, \mathbb{C})$ that is closed under complex conjugation.

steps.slogan: Show that $e_1(x) = e^{ix}$ separates the points of the circle.
steps.detail: If $e^{ix} = e^{iy}$, then $x - y \in 2\pi\mathbb{Z}$, so $x$ and $y$ are the same point of $\mathbb{T}$. Hence the subalgebra separates points.

steps.slogan: Conclude density from the complex Stone–Weierstrass theorem.
steps.detail: On a compact Hausdorff space, a unital subalgebra of the continuous complex functions that separates points and is closed under conjugation is dense in the sup norm. So some trigonometric polynomial is within $\varepsilon$ of $f$ everywhere.

concepts.c:continuous-function: Only continuous functions on the circle can be uniform limits here.
concepts.c:uniform-convergence: The approximation is in the sup norm, uniform in $x$.
concepts.c:trigonometric-polynomial: These are the approximating functions, and they form the subalgebra.
concepts.c:circle: Periodic functions live on the compact circle.
concepts.c:subalgebra: Closure under products is what Stone–Weierstrass requires.

proofs.name: Fejér kernel
proofs.slogan: Convolve $f$ with the Fejér kernel, a positive approximate identity, and use uniform continuity to show that these Cesàro means converge uniformly.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, with the explicit approximants $\sigma_N f$, the Cesàro means of the Fourier series of $f$.

roles.why: Continuity on the compact circle gives uniform continuity for the near part and boundedness for the far part.
Periodicity makes the convolution over one period well defined.

steps.slogan: Define the Fejér kernel $F_N$ and record its three properties.
steps.detail: Let $F_N(x) = \sum_{|n| \le N} \big(1 - \frac{|n|}{N+1}\big) e^{inx} = \frac{1}{N+1} \Big(\frac{\sin((N+1)x/2)}{\sin(x/2)}\Big)^2$. Then $F_N \ge 0$, $\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} F_N = 1$, and $F_N(x) \le \frac{1}{(N+1)\sin^2(\delta/2)}$ for $\delta \le |x| \le \pi$.

steps.slogan: Form the [convolution](c:convolution) $\sigma_N f = f * F_N$, which is a trigonometric polynomial.
steps.detail: Let $\sigma_N f(x) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x - t) F_N(t)\,dt$, defined because $f$ is periodic. Expanding $F_N$ gives $\sigma_N f(x) = \sum_{|n| \le N} \big(1 - \frac{|n|}{N+1}\big) \hat f(n) e^{inx}$, the Cesàro mean of the [Fourier series](c:fourier-series).

steps.slogan: Bound the error integral near $t = 0$ by uniform continuity.
steps.detail: Since $F_N \ge 0$ has mean $1$, $|\sigma_N f(x) - f(x)| \le \frac{1}{2\pi}\int |f(x - t) - f(x)| F_N(t)\,dt$. [Uniform continuity](c:uniform-continuity) gives $\delta > 0$ with $|f(x - t) - f(x)| < \varepsilon/2$ for $|t| < \delta$, so that part is below $\varepsilon/2$.

steps.slogan: Bound the far part by the decay of $F_N$ for large $N$.
steps.detail: For $\delta \le |t| \le \pi$, the integrand is at most $2\|f\|_\infty / ((N+1)\sin^2(\delta/2))$, which is below $\varepsilon/2$ for large $N$, uniformly in $x$. So $\|\sigma_N f - f\|_\infty < \varepsilon$, and $\sigma_N f$ is the required trigonometric polynomial.

concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity gives uniform continuity and boundedness on one period.
concepts.c:uniform-convergence: The Cesàro means converge to $f$ uniformly.
concepts.c:trigonometric-polynomial: Each Cesàro mean is a trigonometric polynomial of degree $N$.
concepts.c:convolution: Averaging $f$ against the kernel produces the approximants.
concepts.c:fourier-series: The approximants are Cesàro means of the Fourier series.
concepts.c:uniform-continuity: One $\delta$ works for every $x$, which makes the bound uniform.

statement: Let $(X, d)$ be a nonempty [complete metric space](c:complete-metric-space) and $T\colon X \to X$ a [contraction](c:contraction-mapping): $d(Tx, Ty) \le k\,d(x, y)$ with a constant $0 \le k < 1$. Then $T$ has a unique [fixed point](c:fixed-point) $x^*$, and for every $x_0 \in X$ the iterates $x_n = T^n x_0$ converge to $x^*$ with $d(x_n, x^*) \le k^n d(x_0, x_1)/(1 - k)$.

hypotheses.text: The space $X$ is nonempty.
The metric space $X$ is [complete](c:complete-metric-space).
The map $T$ is a [contraction](c:contraction-mapping) with a constant $k \in [0, 1)$.

conclusion: $T$ has exactly one fixed point $x^*$, and $d(T^n x_0, x^*) \le k^n d(x_0, Tx_0)/(1 - k)$ for every $x_0 \in X$ and every $n$.

formal.difference: The declaration works in an extended metric space from a start point $x$ with $d(x, Tx) < \infty$ and gives existence, convergence and the rate. Uniqueness is the separate declaration ContractingWith.fixedPoint_unique'.

proofs.name: Picard iteration
proofs.slogan: Iterate the contraction from any point, show that the iterates form a Cauchy sequence with geometric bounds, and pass to the limit.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; the case $k = 0$, where $T$ is constant, is included.

roles.why: A start point $x_0$ exists, so the iteration can begin.
Completeness gives the limit of the Cauchy sequence of iterates.
The factor $k < 1$ gives geometric decay, continuity of $T$ and uniqueness.

steps.slogan: Bound consecutive distances by $d(x_{n+1}, x_n) \le k^n d(x_1, x_0)$.
steps.detail: For $n \ge 1$, $d(x_{n+1}, x_n) = d(Tx_n, Tx_{n-1}) \le k\, d(x_n, x_{n-1})$. Induction on $n$ gives the bound.

steps.slogan: Sum the geometric bounds to show that $(x_n)$ is a [Cauchy sequence](c:cauchy-sequence).
steps.detail: For $m > n$, the triangle inequality and step 1 give $d(x_n, x_m) \le \sum_{j=n}^{m-1} k^j d(x_1, x_0) \le k^n d(x_0, x_1)/(1 - k)$. Since $k < 1$, the right side tends to $0$.

steps.slogan: Take the limit $x^*$ and let $m \to \infty$ in the Cauchy estimate.
steps.detail: Completeness gives $x^* = \lim x_m$. Letting $m \to \infty$ in step 2, continuity of $d$ gives $d(x_n, x^*) \le k^n d(x_0, x_1)/(1 - k)$.

steps.slogan: Pass to the limit in $x_{n+1} = Tx_n$ to get $Tx^* = x^*$.
steps.detail: A contraction is Lipschitz, hence continuous. So $Tx^* = \lim Tx_n = \lim x_{n+1} = x^*$, and $x^*$ is a [fixed point](c:fixed-point).

steps.slogan: Compare any fixed point $y$ with $x^*$ to show uniqueness.
steps.detail: If $Ty = y$, then $d(x^*, y) = d(Tx^*, Ty) \le k\, d(x^*, y)$. Since $k < 1$, this forces $d(x^*, y) = 0$, so $y = x^*$.

concepts.c:complete-metric-space: Completeness supplies the limit of the iterates.
concepts.c:contraction-mapping: The contraction factor gives geometric decay of the steps.
concepts.c:fixed-point: The limit of the iterates is the fixed point.
concepts.c:cauchy-sequence: Geometric bounds make the iterates a Cauchy sequence.

statement: Let $X$ be a real [random variable](c:random-variable), $\varepsilon \in \mathbb{R}$ and $t \ge 0$ with $E[e^{tX}] < \infty$. Then $P(X \ge \varepsilon) \le e^{-t\varepsilon} E[e^{tX}]$. Hence $P(X \ge \varepsilon) \le \inf_{t \ge 0} e^{-t\varepsilon} M_X(t)$, where $M_X(t) = E[e^{tX}]$ is the [moment generating function](c:moment-generating-function).

hypotheses.text: The parameter satisfies $t \ge 0$.
The [expected value](c:expected-value) $E[e^{tX}]$ is finite.

conclusion: $P(X \ge \varepsilon) \le e^{-t\varepsilon} M_X(t)$ for each such $t$, and so $P(X \ge \varepsilon) \le \inf_{t \ge 0} e^{-t\varepsilon} M_X(t)$.

formal.difference: The declaration holds for any finite measure in place of a probability measure. It gives the bound for one $t$; the infimum over $t$ is not part of it.

proofs.name: Markov's inequality for the exponential
proofs.slogan: Turn the tail event into an event about $e^{tX}$ and apply Markov's inequality to this nonnegative variable.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; for $t = 0$ the bound reads $P(X \ge \varepsilon) \le 1$. Values of $t$ with $M_X(t) = \infty$ give a trivial bound in the infimum.

roles.why: For $t \ge 0$ the map $x \mapsto e^{tx}$ is nondecreasing, so the event inclusion holds.
A finite mean of $e^{tX}$ makes the Markov bound finite.

steps.slogan: Include the event $\{X \ge \varepsilon\}$ in the event $\{e^{tX} \ge e^{t\varepsilon}\}$.
steps.detail: For $t \ge 0$ the [exponential function](c:exponential-function) $x \mapsto e^{tx}$ is nondecreasing, so $X \ge \varepsilon$ implies $e^{tX} \ge e^{t\varepsilon}$. For $t = 0$ the second event is the whole space.

steps.slogan: Apply Markov's inequality to $e^{tX}$ at the level $e^{t\varepsilon}$.
steps.detail: The variable $e^{tX}$ is positive with finite mean $M_X(t)$. Markov's inequality gives $P(e^{tX} \ge e^{t\varepsilon}) \le E[e^{tX}]/e^{t\varepsilon} = e^{-t\varepsilon} M_X(t)$.

steps.slogan: Combine the inclusion with the Markov bound by monotonicity of $P$.
steps.detail: Monotonicity of probability and step 1 give $P(X \ge \varepsilon) \le P(e^{tX} \ge e^{t\varepsilon})$. Step 2 bounds the right side by $e^{-t\varepsilon} M_X(t)$.

steps.slogan: Take the infimum of the bound over all $t \ge 0$.
steps.detail: The left side does not depend on $t$, and step 3 holds for every $t \ge 0$ with $M_X(t) < \infty$; for the other $t$ the bound is $\infty$. So $P(X \ge \varepsilon) \le \inf_{t \ge 0} e^{-t\varepsilon} M_X(t)$.

concepts.c:random-variable: The bound controls the upper tail of this variable.
concepts.c:moment-generating-function: The bound is stated through the moment generating function.
concepts.c:expected-value: Markov's inequality bounds a tail probability by an expected value.
concepts.c:exponential-function: A monotone exponential turns the tail event into a Markov event.

statement: Let $X$ have density $f(x; \theta)$ for $\theta$ in an open interval $\Theta$, with the regularity conditions below, and let $T(X)$ be an [unbiased estimator](c:unbiased-estimator) of $g(\theta)$ with finite [variance](c:variance). Then $\mathrm{Var}_\theta(T) \ge g'(\theta)^2/I(\theta)$, where $I(\theta) = E_\theta\big[(\partial_\theta \log f(X; \theta))^2\big]$ is the [Fisher information](c:fisher-information).

hypotheses.text: The densities $f(x; \theta) > 0$ have a common support and are differentiable in $\theta \in \Theta$.
Differentiation in $\theta$ passes under the integral sign in $\int f\,dx = 1$ and in $\int T f\,dx = g(\theta)$.
The [Fisher information](c:fisher-information) satisfies $0 < I(\theta) < \infty$.
The estimator is [unbiased](c:unbiased-estimator), $E_\theta[T] = g(\theta)$ for all $\theta \in \Theta$, and $\mathrm{Var}_\theta(T) < \infty$.

proofs.name: Score and Cauchy–Schwarz
proofs.slogan: Show that the score has mean zero and covariance $g'(\theta)$ with the estimator, then bound this covariance by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality.
proofs.scope: The one-parameter case at a fixed $\theta \in \Theta$; discrete families work the same way with sums.

roles.why: Differentiability with a common support makes the score $\partial_\theta \log f$ defined.
Differentiation under the integral gives the mean of the score and its covariance with the estimator.
Finite positive information is the variance of the score, and it allows the final division.
Unbiasedness gives the identity whose derivative is $g'(\theta)$, and finite variance makes Cauchy–Schwarz apply.

steps.slogan: Define the score $S = \partial_\theta \log f(X; \theta)$ and show that its mean is zero.
steps.detail: Since $\partial_\theta f = S f$, differentiating $\int f\,dx = 1$ under the integral gives $E_\theta[S] = \int \partial_\theta f\,dx = 0$. So $\mathrm{Var}_\theta(S) = E_\theta[S^2] = I(\theta)$.

steps.slogan: Differentiate the unbiasedness identity to get $\mathrm{Cov}_\theta(T, S) = g'(\theta)$.
steps.detail: Differentiating $\int T f\,dx = g(\theta)$ under the integral gives $g'(\theta) = \int T S f\,dx = E_\theta[TS]$. Since $E_\theta[S] = 0$, this equals $\mathrm{Cov}_\theta(T, S)$.

steps.slogan: Bound the covariance by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality.
steps.detail: The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality for the centered variables $T - g(\theta)$ and $S$ gives $g'(\theta)^2 = \mathrm{Cov}_\theta(T, S)^2 \le \mathrm{Var}_\theta(T)\,\mathrm{Var}_\theta(S) = \mathrm{Var}_\theta(T)\, I(\theta)$.

steps.slogan: Divide by the positive Fisher information to get the bound.
steps.detail: Since $0 < I(\theta) < \infty$, dividing step 3 by $I(\theta)$ gives $\mathrm{Var}_\theta(T) \ge g'(\theta)^2/I(\theta)$. For $g(\theta) = \theta$ the bound is $1/I(\theta)$.

concepts.c:unbiased-estimator: Unbiasedness gives the identity whose derivative is $g'(\theta)$.
concepts.c:variance: The theorem bounds the variance of the estimator from below.
concepts.c:fisher-information: The information is the variance of the score.

source.note: The classical score argument, as in Casella and Berger, Statistical Inference, 2nd edition, theorem 7.3.9.
